sections.overview: The little grebe is the smallest of the grebes in Britain: a shy, dumpy diving bird of ponds and lakes. It is often hidden among vegetation and betrays itself by its high-pitched, whinnying trill.
sections.identification: A small, dumpy grebe whose rear often looks fluffy, with an adult weight of about 225 g and a wing length near 104 mm; one account gives a body length of about 29 cm. In summer it has a bright chestnut throat and cheeks and a pale gape patch at the base of the bill.
sections.habitat: In Britain and Ireland it breeds most often on lakes and ponds, including small farm ponds and urban parks. In winter it also uses rivers, streams and some brackish and coastal sites.
sections.diet: A field guide from Kenya describes a diet of insects and their larvae, small fish, frogs and tadpoles, small crustaceans and molluscs, all caught by diving.
sections.behavior: It dives readily when disturbed and surfaces unseen some way off, rather than flying. Its feet are set far back on the body, so it is awkward on land. Birds that breed in Britain make short moves to wintering sites, and others arrive from elsewhere.
sections.reproduction: The nest is a floating platform of vegetation anchored to submerged plants. There are typically two broods, each of four to six eggs, incubated by both sexes for 20–21 days. The downy chicks leave the nest quickly and sometimes ride on a parent’s back; they fledge after about 44–48 days. Breeding typically starts at one year.
sections.ecology: In Britain, nests succeed more often on ponds and lakes than on rivers and streams, where fluctuating water levels cause flooding failures. In Africa, tawny eagles, herons and Cape clawless otters are among its predators. The oldest ringed bird in Britain lived just over six years.
sections.conservation: The IUCN Red List classes it as Least Concern. The UK breeding population was about 5,500 pairs in 2016, with some 16,000 birds in winter. It is Green-listed in the UK, after a spell on the Amber list during a decline in 2009–15, and has been broadly stable in Europe since 1990.
